explication:
<explanation>
1. Identify the project type and purpose  
   - OpenManus is an open-source Python framework for building and running general AI agents. It provides:  
     • A command-line interface (CLI) to kick off different agent workflows (single-agent, multi-agent “MCP”, unstable multi-agent flows).  
     • A modular “agent + flow + tool + sandbox” architecture that lets you orchestrate LLM calls, tool invocations, browser automation, code execution in isolation, and more.  

2. Analyze the file structure  
   - Top-level entries:  
     • main.py / run_flow.py / run_mcp.py – CLI entrypoints  
     • app/ – core library  
       – agent/ – different agent implementations (browser, data_analysis, SWE, toolcall, React, Manus)  
       – flow/ – base classes, flow_factory, built-in planning flow  
       – prompt/ – prompt templates for each agent type and sub-module  
       – tool/ – tool wrappers (bash, browser_use_tool, python_execute, search, visualization, etc.)  
       – sandbox/ – isolation layer (client, core manager, docker/terminal sandbox)  
       – mcp/ – multi-choice picker server & client  
       – llm.py, bedrock.py, config.py – LLM adapter & configuration  
       – logger.py, exceptions.py, schema.py  
     • config/ – example TOML files for different LLM backends  
     • tests/ – unit tests for sandbox and other components  
     • assets/, examples/, workspace/ – static assets and usage examples  

3. Key architectural insights from README  
   - Uses a plug-in pattern: you can register new agents, new tools, new flows.  
   - Supports multiple LLM backends via a common interface (OpenAI, Anthropic, Azure, etc.)  
   - Provides a sandboxed environment (via Docker or terminal emulation) to safely execute code/commands.  
   - Offers both single-agent and multi-agent (“MCP”) workflows, configurable via command line.  

4. How to diagram this architecture  
   a. Main components  
      1. CLI Launchers (main.py, run_flow.py, run_mcp.py)  
      2. Configuration Loader (config.py → loads TOML → supplies API keys, model settings)  
      3. Flow Manager (flow_factory + Flow classes)  
      4. Agent Modules (agent/*)  
      5. Prompt Templates (prompt/*)  
      6. LLM Adapter (app/llm.py + bedrock.py) → External LLM APIs  
      7. Tool Registry (tool/*) → built-in tools (search, bash, Python exec, browser, charts)  
      8. Sandbox Layer (sandbox/client + core/manager + docker/terminal)  
      9. MCP Server (mcp/server.py) + MCP Client  
     10. Logger & Schema & Exceptions  
     11. External Services: LLM endpoints, Web browsers (Playwright), Search engines  

   b. Relationships & Data Flows  
      • CLI → Configuration Loader → Flow Manager  
      • Flow Manager instantiates one or more Agent(s) → selects Prompt(s) → renders prompt → LLM Adapter → external API → returns LLM response → Agent interprets response  
      • If Agent triggers a Tool, it goes through the Tool Registry → may call Sandbox Layer to execute code/commands securely → returns result to Agent  
      • Agent may trigger multiple tools or multi-agent coordination via the MCP Server/Client  
      • All interactions logged via Logger  

   c. Architectural patterns & principles  
      - Modular plug-in architecture (agents, flows, tools are all swappable / extendable)  
      - Factory pattern for flows (flow_factory)  
      - Adapter pattern for LLM backends  
      - Isolation of side-effects via sandbox  
      - Clear separation of concerns: prompting vs. execution vs. orchestration  

   d. Key technologies/frameworks  
      - Python 3.12, Typing, dataclasses  
      - TOML for config  
      - Playwright for browser automation  
      - Docker (optional) for sandbox  
      - HTTP server (Flask-like) for MCP server  
      - Standard logging  

5. Tailoring the diagram for an open-source AI-agent framework  
   - Emphasize the core pipeline: CLI → Flow → Agent → Prompt → LLM → Agent → Tool → Sandbox → back to Agent → final output  
   - Highlight extension points: where to drop in a new Agent class, a new Tool module, or a new Flow definition  
   - Show optional branches: single agent vs. MCP vs. planning flow  

6. Diagramming guidelines  
   - Use rectangular boxes for components (e.g., “Flow Manager”, “Agent: DataAnalysis”, “Tool: PythonExecute”)  
   - Use directional arrows to indicate data/control flow (e.g., from “Agent” to “LLM Adapter” to “OpenAI API”)  
   - Group related components in swimlanes or colored zones:  
     • Configuration & Setup (config loader, logger) – color A  
     • Orchestration Layer (CLI, Flow Manager, MCP) – color B  
     • Core Logic (Agents, Prompts, LLM Adapter) – color C  
     • Execution Layer (Tools, Sandbox) – color D  
   - Label arrows with the payload (e.g., “prompt text”, “API response”, “tool command”)  
   - Use different shapes (ovals for external systems, cylinders for persistent config/tests)  

7. Essential elements to include  
   - Clear component names matching folder/module names  
   - Labeled arrows for data/control flows  
   - Color coding or swimlanes for component categories  
   - Notes on extension points (e.g., “new agent goes here”)  

By following this breakdown and structuring your diagram around these layers and flows, you will capture the full richness of OpenManus’s modular agent framework without over-complicating the visualization.  
</explanation>
